extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of psychology, literature, and humor; readers studying techniques of wit (e.g., Freud readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Close analytic taxonomy of the technical devices that produce wit (condensation, word-formation, double-meaning, puns, displacements) with examples and theoretical commentary. The page explicates specific sub-techniques and their relation to a unifying principle (economy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation with mixed word-formation
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of reduction in which two thoughts are fused by creating a mixed word-formation (substitutive formation) that compresses fuller phrasing into a compact expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: portmanteau-like formations and compound words that merge ideas; condensation produces brevity that is specifically witty rather than mere laconism. The author treats this as one principal technical means of wit; compare with dream condensation. Scoring note: identify merged elements and the omitted thought they substitute for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation with modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Condensation achieved by a small modification of an expected phrase (replacement/substitution) that alludes to an omitted abusive or contrasting thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a great future behind him' (replacement of 'before' by 'behind'), 'going backward on all-fours' (addition implying animality). Technique often leaves an implication/allusion to a fuller (often critical) thought. Scoring: detect the omitted thought and how the modification stands for it; note that the modification can be a single-word change that triggers the second thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation / substitutive formation (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The broader category wherein verbal economy (compression) substitutes for a more explicit statement; condensation is the chief category unifying many techniques of wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud argues condensation (a compressing or economic tendency) underlies many wit techniques. Evaluate how the utterance saves the expression of a second thought by containing it implicitly. Caveat: not all brevity equals wit — it must be this specific substitutive economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-division (whole vs part / charade technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a name or word both as a whole and then divided into syllables or parts so that the divided parts yield a different meaning (a charade-like use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Rousseau' → 'roux et sot' (red-haired and foolish), Buonaparte/Buonaparte pun. Technique depends on recognizable syllable-division producing a new sense. Scoring: check that the syllabic split produces a new, contextually apt meaning and that the whole/divided uses are deliberately juxtaposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold application: same material, change of order
rubrics_metrics.description: Using identical words/material twice in a sentence but altering order to shift sense between subjects/objects (syntactic exchange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Put in a dinner and a speech appears — put in a speech and a dinner appears.' Technique: exchange of places yields contrapuntal meaning. Scoring: identify the parallel phrases and how reordering transfers attributes between referents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold application: slight modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same material with a very slight change (one letter, small edit) to convert one meaning into another closely related meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one-letter change that differentiates two senses or social standings; 'antisemitism' variant example. The slighter the change, the stronger the technical effect. Scoring: note minimal surface change and maximal semantic shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifold application: whole words in full vs 'colorless' sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same words in two senses: once with a full concrete meaning and once with a colorless/grammatical or idiomatic sense, producing an unexpected overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'undertaker' (funeral manager) + 'carry out' used literally → witty effect; 'un-' prefix in 'unremitting' read as negation vs part of lexical item. Scoring: detect the two readings (full vs grammatical) and the surprise produced by literalizing a normally idiomatic element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning: name and verbal significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A double reading that exploits a name as both a proper noun and as words with independent verbal or lexical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: puns on names in Shakespeare quotations or Heine's Banko/Banquo. Scoring: identify the dual referents (person vs semantic content) and how context supports both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning: metaphorical vs verbal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A double sense where a term has both a literal/verbal sense and a metaphorical or figurative sense, enabling witty overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'holding the mirror up to nature' — mirror as object and metaphor for representation. Scoring: show how both senses are coherent in context and produce the ironic or epigrammatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: True double meaning / play on words
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal case in which the identical word, in the same wording, legitimately expresses two different meanings simultaneously (a genuine play on words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'C'est le premier vol de l'aigle' (vol = flight/theft) or 'Le roi n'est pas sujet' (subject/vasal). Scoring: verify both senses are grammatically and contextually plausible and that their coexistence yields the wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity (sexual or general double sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-meaning instances where one meaning (often sexual) is ambiguous with the ordinary sense; the joke relies on this uncertainty/possible reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The army does not believe in her innocence' — innocence/nubility ambiguity. Scoring: show that both readings are plausible and that the comic effect hinges on the listener's inability to choose definitively between senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning with allusion (unequal prominence of senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where one sense of a double-meaning is more obtrusive and the other is veiled or alluded to; the less prominent meaning is accessible by inference or cultural knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I never aspired as high as that' — surface sense masks sexual innuendo. Scoring: determine the dominant sense and the veiled one; note how concealment contributes to wit (allusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns (sound-based play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit that depends chiefly on phonetic or orthographic similarity between distinct words (sound-play), often considered the lowest form because it operates on sound rather than internal lexical duality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Humbug', 'rerotten', vowel-modification puns; student pranks on Agassiz. Fischer's view: puns are poor plays on the sound rather than on the word itself. Scoring: measure reliance on mere phonetic resemblance and perceived 'cheapness' versus depth of conceptual condensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to economy (unity principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud's proposed unifying principle: wit techniques manifest an economy of expression — condensation that saves the articulation of a second thought by embedding or implying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply as higher-level criterion: ask what thought is economized/omitted and how the utterance contains that thought implicitly. Caveat: economy alone is not sufficient — the economy must be of the special type that produces pleasure; not every brevity is witty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy with dream-work condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The observation that the condensation process in dreams (dream-work) produces similar substitutive formations and abbreviations as wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dream examples (composed names/objects, composite figures) to analyze analogous mechanisms in wit. Scoring: identify parallel structures (composition, modification) and consider psychoanalytic implications for latent content vs manifest expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacements / unclassifiable techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of witticism whose technique resists neat classification under the earlier groups—displacement effects, unexpected corrective rejoinders, or otherwise subtle inversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Heine/Soulie 'Golden Calf' rejoinder 'he must be older than that' — technique unclear. Treat as a category signaling limits of taxonomy; scoring: note the evasive rhetorical move and document why it doesn't fit other types.
